title: What happens when a `Serializable` class contains a member that is not serializable (`NotSerializableException`), and how do you fix it (make it serializable, mark `transient`, or custom `writeObject`/`readObject`)?
shortTitle: What happens with a non-serializable member inside a Serializable class?

s1_definition.profdef: When a class implements Serializable but holds a reference to an object whose class does not implement Serializable, serialization fails at runtime with a NotSerializableException naming the offending class, because the serialization engine must walk the entire reachable object graph and every referenced object's class must also be serializable. There are three standard remedies: make the referenced class implement Serializable if you own it and it is safe to persist, mark the field transient so the engine skips it entirely, or take manual control with custom writeObject and readObject methods that serialize a safe representation and rebuild the field on the way back.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, sealing Rajesh's account file into a mailing packet requires every attached document to carry the signed consent form that says it may be flattened and mailed. If one attached document, say a live database connection slip, has no consent form, the mail room stops and names that exact document as the blocker. You can fix it three ways: get that document its own consent form, remove it from the packet because it should not travel anyway, or write a short handwritten note describing how to recreate that document at the destination.
s1_definition.oneliner: A non-serializable member inside a Serializable class throws NotSerializableException naming it, and the three fixes are make it serializable, mark it transient, or handle it manually with writeObject and readObject.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** When a class implements Serializable but holds a reference to an object whose class does not implement Serializable, serialization fails at runtime with a NotSerializableException naming the offending class, because the serialization engine must walk the entire reachable object graph and every referenced object's class must also be serializable. There are three standard remedies: make the referenced class implement Serializable if you own it and it is safe to persist, mark the field transient so the engine skips it entirely, or take manual control with custom writeObject and readObject methods that serialize a safe representation and rebuild the field on the way back.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, sealing Rajesh's account file into a mailing packet requires every attached document to carry the signed consent form that says it may be flattened and mailed. If one attached document, say a live database connection slip, has no consent form, the mail room stops and names that exact document as the blocker. You can fix it three ways: get that document its own consent form, remove it from the packet because it should not travel anyway, or write a short handwritten note describing how to recreate that document at the destination.

**One line to remember:** A non-serializable member inside a Serializable class throws NotSerializableException naming it, and the three fixes are make it serializable, mark it transient, or handle it manually with writeObject and readObject.

sections.s2_technical:
Serialization is recursive. Starting from the root object, the engine serializes each non-static, non-transient field, and for any field that is a reference it recurses into the referenced object. For that recursion to succeed, every class it reaches must implement Serializable. The moment it reaches an object whose class does not, it throws `java.io.NotSerializableException` and the message is the fully qualified name of that class, which is your primary diagnostic clue.

The first fix is to make the member serializable. If you own the class and its state is meaningful and safe to persist, add `implements Serializable` and, ideally, a stable serialVersionUID. For example, if an Account references an Owner and the Owner should travel with the account, make Owner serializable.

The second fix is transient. If the field is runtime-only, holds a resource, or is sensitive, declare it transient so the engine skips it:

```java
private transient java.sql.Connection dbConnection; // resource, never serialize
private transient String sessionToken;              // sensitive, never persist
```

On deserialization a transient field is left at its default value, which is null for references and zero for numeric primitives, so you re-establish it afterward if needed.

The third fix is custom writeObject and readObject. When you need the field's information but it cannot be serialized directly, you serialize a safe substitute and rebuild the field on read. The `writeObject` method starts with `defaultWriteObject()` to write all normal fields, then writes your substitute, and `readObject` starts with `defaultReadObject()` then reads the substitute and reconstructs the field.

```java
private transient ExchangeRateService rateService; // not serializable

private void writeObject(java.io.ObjectOutputStream out) throws java.io.IOException {
    out.defaultWriteObject();            // writes the normal fields
    out.writeUTF(rateService.region());  // write a safe, small substitute
}
private void readObject(java.io.ObjectInputStream in)
        throws java.io.IOException, ClassNotFoundException {
    in.defaultReadObject();              // reads the normal fields
    String region = in.readUTF();        // read the substitute
    this.rateService = ExchangeRateService.forRegion(region); // rebuild
}
```

A senior point is to choose the fix by intent. Make it serializable only when the data should truly travel and is safe. Use transient for resources, caches, and secrets. Use custom methods when the field is essential but the object itself is not directly serializable, for example a service handle you can recreate from a small key. Another senior point is that marking a field transient does not lose the concept, only the live object, so you must handle rebuilding it, otherwise after deserialization it is null and the first use throws a NullPointerException.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — An Account referenced a live database connection object that is not serializable, and caching the account failed with NotSerializableException. This is exactly the transient fix for a resource.

Problem 2 — The same Account referenced an Owner that should travel with it, and until Owner implemented Serializable, serialization failed. This is exactly the make-it-serializable fix.

Problem 3 — The Account referenced an exchange-rate service handle that cannot be serialized but is needed, and we rebuilt it from a small region key using custom writeObject and readObject. This is exactly the manual-control fix.

The code defines a Serializable `Owner`, an `ExchangeRateService` that is not serializable but recreatable, and an `Account` that applies all three fixes, driven by a `NonSerializableMemberDemo` main class.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is an account referencing a serializable Owner, a transient sensitive sessionToken, and a transient non-serializable ExchangeRateService created for region IN.

Step 1: Serialization starts at the account. It writes the accountId and balance, then recurses into the owner, which is serializable, so the owner's name and panId are written.

Step 2: The engine reaches the transient sessionToken and the transient rateService and skips both, because transient fields are not serialized.

Step 3: Because the account defines writeObject, after the default fields the custom code writes the region key IN as a small substitute for the non-serializable service.

Step 4: On deserialization, defaultReadObject restores accountId, balance, and owner. The sessionToken stays null because it was transient.

Step 5: The custom readObject reads the region key IN and calls the factory to rebuild a fresh ExchangeRateService for region IN, so the field is usable again rather than null.

```
Oct 30, 2026 ... INFO: Serialized OK, length = 300
Oct 30, 2026 ... INFO: Owner survived: Rajesh Kumar
Oct 30, 2026 ... WARNING: sessionToken after deserialize (transient) = null
Oct 30, 2026 ... INFO: rateService rebuilt for region = IN
```


sections.s6_takeaway:
Serialization is recursive, so when a Serializable class holds a reference to an object whose class is not serializable, the engine walks into that object, finds no permission, and throws a NotSerializableException whose message is the fully qualified name of the offending class. That name is my first diagnostic clue, and the fix depends on what the field actually is.

The first fix is to make the member serializable. If I own the class and its state should genuinely travel with the owner and is safe to persist, I add implements Serializable and a stable serialVersionUID. In my banking work this applied to an Owner object that should always accompany the account.

The second fix is transient. If the field is a live resource like a database connection, a cache, or a secret like a session token, it should never be persisted, so I mark it transient and the engine skips it. The catch is that after deserialization a transient reference is null, so if the application needs it I must re-establish it, otherwise the first use throws a NullPointerException.

The third fix is custom writeObject and readObject for a field that is essential but not directly serializable. In writeObject I call defaultWriteObject and then write a small safe substitute, and in readObject I call defaultReadObject and then rebuild the field from that substitute. I used this for an exchange-rate service handle: I wrote only its region key and recreated the handle through a factory on the way back. So my complete answer is that a non-serializable member throws NotSerializableException naming it, and I choose among making it serializable, marking it transient, or handling it manually based on whether the data should travel, should be dropped, or should be rebuilt.

---

keyPoints: NotSerializableException thrown at runtime during writeObject()
Fix 1: make the member transient — skip it during serialization
Fix 2: make the member class implement Serializable
Fix 3: implement custom writeObject/readObject to handle it manually
